Oct 23 : The Asian Football Confederation approved sweeping changes to its statutes on Friday, including a decision to move the Asian Cup to even-numbered years from 2032 as part of efforts to align with FIFA's evolving international calendar. The amendments were unanimously approved at an Extraordinary Congress in Tokyo and introduced measures designed to keep the AFC's electoral cycle in sync with its competitions calendar amid upcoming changes to FIFA's schedule. Under the new framework, the Asian Cup, traditionally staged in odd-numbered years, will switch to an even-year cycle beginning with the 2032 tournament. The next edition is set to take place from January to February 2027 in Saudi Arabia. The AFC said the move would ensure its leadership cycle remains aligned with the confederation's flagship national-team competition and allow its executive committee to retain oversight of the event during key stages of its organisation.

However, under the new arrangements, those elected will take office on January 1, 2028, for a four-year term running through 2032. The current executive members will remain in place until the end of 2027.

LONDON, Oct 23 : Global indoor fitness race company Hyrox is teaming up with new player Xenom to expand participation and maybe one day even be accepted into the Olympics, the companies' executives say. Hyrox, founded in Hamburg, Germany, in 2017, and Xenom, a CrossFit-inspired platform founded in 2026, announced a strategic partnership earlier this month to work together on marketing, events and education.  The founders of Hyrox, Olympic gold medallist Moritz Fuerste and entrepreneur Christian Toetzke, have invested in Xenom, the latter company said in its announcement, without giving any financial details.  Their shared goal, it said, was "making fitness the largest sport on earth."

Hyrox joins a board that includes US investment firm WndrCo founded by former Walt Disney Studios Chairman Jeffrey Katzenberg and former Dropbox CFO Sujay Jaswa, who led Xenom's $15 million seed round.  “It made a lot of sense to us, the partnership. We exist in separate but connected markets on the same spectrum of fitness and we see a future where people will move around that spectrum," Xenom CEO Keith Barlow told Reuters.  A Xenom competition involves athletes participating in 10 fixed standardised events across two days.  That is similar to Hyrox's standard fixed eight-event format which combines running and functional workouts, offering participants four different racing categories. Mass-participation fitness events are increasingly popular.   “We're planning to end up somewhere at 2.2 million participants for this running season. 2.5-ish for the calendar year (20)27,” Fuerste, a former German hockey player, told Reuters about Hyrox.  FITNESS AT THE OLYMPICS? Xenom, which held its inaugural event Dallas, Texas, in June followed by an event in London, has seen early growth. “We had just over 400 athletes in Dallas and we had 560-ish in London. So about 30 per cent growth on the first two events and then coming into Miami, we've got really high expectations,” Barlow said, as Xenom prepares for its Miami event in December and then its first full international season in 2027 opening in Malaga. As Hyrox continues to attract more participants across the world, so does its expansion ambitions.  With over 100 events in cities including London and Rio de Janeiro, Fuerste wants to enlarge Hyrox’s footprint in Latin America. “I think probably South America is a region where we can grow. Apart from Argentina, Brazil, then middle America, Mexico. There is a little bit more room to grow there.” Hyrox would also love to see fitness become an Olympic discipline – possibly by Brisbane 2032. "That's the big goal and the aspiration that we have. And we are working on the technicalities behind that …. Is it super likely? I don't know,” said Fuerste.

Source: Reuters

PARIS: British and French jets flew together over the Mediterranean in their first joint exercise involving France's airborne nuclear capability, Paris said on Friday (Oct 23), underscoring their cooperation at a time of friction with Russia. The two allies agreed in July 2025 to reinforce cooperation over their nuclear arsenals in response to growing threats to Europe and uncertainty over their US ally.   "Having independent nuclear forces does not preclude coordination," said French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin. "Our nuclear cooperation with the United Kingdom continues to deepen: on Tuesday evening, British Typhoons took part for the very first time in a French nuclear exercise alongside Rafales (warplanes)."

After taking off from the Saint-Dizier air base in northeastern France, the French jets were escorted by British RAF Typhoon fighters, simulating a nuclear strike in an exercise called "Rummy", France's Armed Forces ministry said. "In an increasingly dangerous world, our adversaries should be in no doubt: the United Kingdom and France stand together in their commitment to European security and to maintaining the deterrence that has helped preserve peace for generations," added British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting. France's President Emmanuel Macron said in March that Paris would expand its nuclear arsenal and launched an initiative offering European partners joint exercises and possible short-term deployment of French nuclear-capable assets on their territory.  France spends roughly €5.6 billion (US$6.04 billion) a year to maintain its stockpile of 290 submarine- and air-launched weapons — the world's fourth-largest arsenal.  Britain has 225 nuclear warheads.  In comparison, Russia and the United States have more than 5,000 each.

CAPE TOWN, Oct 23 : Quick bowler Kagiso Rabada's battles with Steve Smith sparked a combustible series the last time Australia played tests in South Africa eight years ago and the pair have resumed their rivalry as the teams head for a decisive contest in Cape Town next week. Rabada returned after a long hamstring injury layoff to help South Africa win by an innings and 31 runs in the second test in Gqeberha on Thursday to square the three-match series and set up a potential thriller at Newlands, starting next Tuesday. Rabada's four second-innings wickets included that of the 37-year-old Smith, who, surprisingly early in his innings, out of character and with Australia in dire straits, attempted an ill-fated hook to a bouncer and top-edged a catch to midwicket. It was an injudicious decision from the former captain, who passed the milestone of 11,000 test runs at St George’s Park but made only three runs in the second innings as he looked out of sorts with a neck complaint.

GETTING BEST PLAYER OUT “He wasn’t 100 per cent fit in the game but we knew he had the ability to knuckle down and be the anchor for them; he’s done it for so long for Australia,” Rabada said in a TV interview. “He’s a top-class player and you can put a lot more pressure on a team when you get their best player out, so he’ll always be a prized wicket playing against Australia.”  Rabada had also dismissed Smith at St George’s Park in 2018, the first of 11 wickets he took in that test, but he collided with the Australian while celebrating taking his wicket and was handed a two-match ban, later downgraded to a fine. The shoulder bump was among several incidents in an ill-spirited series that ended with the infamous ‘Sandpapergate’ ball-tampering scandal after which Smith was stripped of the captaincy and banned for 12 months by Cricket Australia. NO GRUDGES, ONLY TESTOSTERONE Rabada, however, said there were no grudges and that it was part of intense competition. “As an athlete you want to go out and express yourself. There’s no hate off the field or anything like that. It’s a bunch of top-performing athletes who’ve got testosterone to burn. It’s the heat of the moment,” the South African paceman said. Smith has been back to Newlands since the scandal, playing in a T20 international two years after the incident, but this will be his first test at the venue since 2018. Last month he said he had learned from the experience after being sent home in disgrace. "It was certainly a difficult period, particularly the initial period a few days after," Smith told Sydney's Daily Telegraph . "The mental state I was in was not great. That's somewhere I'd like not to get to again, but I certainly learned from that and have been able to move forward with my life. I've tried to kind of erase a lot of 2018 and what happened," he added. "I can't remember a lot about the series. I've tried to block most of it out of my memory bank."

Source: Reuters

Oct 23 : Kenya's world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended after testing positive for the banned blood booster EPO in a sample taken before her Sydney Marathon victory, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said on Friday. The AIU added that the out-of-competition sample collected in Kenya returned an adverse analytical finding for EPO (erythropoietin), which boosts the production of red blood cells. "I can only say that I feel terrible about what happened and I think it's only right that an athlete who uses the performance enhancing drugs should be disqualified," her agent Gianni Demadonna said in an emailed statement. The 33-year-old is a former Olympic champion and half-marathon world record holder as well as a four-times World Marathon Majors winner.

Oct 23 : Global equity funds attracted inflows for a fifth consecutive week in the week through October 21, as easing Treasury yields and strong early corporate earnings lifted investor sentiment. Global equity funds drew net inflows of $28.16 billion during the week, compared with $19.88 billion in the previous week, LSEG Lipper data showed. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield fell about 15 basis points last week and dropped below the psychologically significant 5 per cent level this week. Fund investors were encouraged by better-than-expected corporate earnings so far this reporting season.

Of the nearly 18 per cent of MSCI All Country World Index constituents that have reported earnings to date, about 73 per cent have exceeded the average analyst estimate, according to LSEG data. The MSCI World Index, however, fell 1.31 per cent on Thursday after Meta reported strong results on Wednesday but unveiled plans to issue non-voting stock, reviving concerns about its growing capital commitments. By region, Asian equity funds attracted $11.53 billion, their largest weekly inflow since at least December 2022. Investors also added $9.14 billion to European equity funds and $5.07 billion to US equity funds. Among sectoral funds, technology attracted $5.05 billion, reversing net sales of $4.77 billion in the previous week. Investors also bought $1.83 billion in healthcare sector funds but sold a notable $1.29 billion in consumer discretionary sector funds. Global bond funds remained popular for a fifth consecutive week, attracting net inflows of $9.44 billion. Swiss franc-denominated bond funds drew $6.8 billion, their largest weekly inflow since at least November 2024. Investors also added a significant $2.78 billion to short-term bond funds, while pulling $1.68 billion from high-yield bond funds and $550 million from government bond funds. Money market funds attracted weekly net inflows of $15.86 billion, following net outflows of $47.51 billion the previous week. Among commodities, gold and other precious metals funds attracted net inflows of $1.29 billion, marking their fifth week of net purchases in the past six weeks. Investors also added $41.5 million to energy funds. Data covering 29,174 emerging market funds showed that investors bought $6.28 billion worth of equity funds — the largest weekly net purchase since August 5. However, they withdrew a marginal $48.72 million from bond funds.

Source: Reuters

BENGALURU, Oct 23 Reuters) - Infosys trimmed its annual revenue growth forecast on Friday despite marginally beating estimates for quarterly revenue after demand from its energy and utility clients picked up. Revenue at India's second-largest IT services provider rose 10.7 per cent to 492.44 billion rupees ($5.19 billion) in the July-September period.  Analysts on average had estimated revenue of 491.32 billion rupees, according to data compiled by LSEG.  The company revised its revenue growth forecast for the fiscal year ending March 2027 to 1 per cent-2 per cent from its earlier estimate of up 1.5 per cent-3 per cent.

Most analysts had expected the company to downgrade the upper-end of the range to 1.5 per cent to 2.5 per cent. The rise of AI has hurt India's $315 billion IT industry, forcing companies to overhaul their business models and offer steep discounts. Despite AI unlocking newer revenue streams, it is challenging the traditional revenue as clients are increasingly tying fees to technology-led productivity gains instead of hours worked.   Peers Tata Consultancy Services and HCLTech both met their revenue estimates earlier this week, but their investors cheered AI revenue uptick with their stocks surging. Revenue from Infosys' energy business, its third-largest revenue contributor, rose 7.3 per cent from a year earlier after stripping out currency fluctuations. The overall revenue rose 1.5 per cent, excluding the currency impact. The Bengaluru-based tech major's net profit rose 6.2 per cent to 78.23 billion rupees in the three-month period, falling below 79.29 billion rupees expected by analysts, as per LSEG-compiled data.  Deal wins stood at $5.2 billion during the quarter, compared with $3.1 billion in the year-ago quarter.  The company's Mumbai-listed shares closed flat ahead of the results, with a basket of IT stocks dropping 0.3 per cent. Oct 23 : Wall Street futures ticked lower on Friday as caution prevailed after a sharp selloff in AI-linked stocks over concerns about the sector's massive funding requirements, while telecom shares slid on fears of increased competition from SpaceX. AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile were down over 3 per cent in premarket trading after a report said SpaceX was in talks with cellular infrastructure companies about launching a nationwide wireless carrier program. US cell tower operators, however, gained from this news, with Crown Castle up 8.5 per cent and American Tower up 5.6 per cent. SpaceX shares gained 2.2 per cent. AI-related shares swung sharply this week, first coming under pressure over CoreWeave's debt burden and the cost of financing AI investment, then rallying on Wednesday after upbeat results from SpaceX and Super Micro.

The gains reversed on Thursday and the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell nearly 3 per cent. The slide accelerated following Meta's nearly 8 per cent decline after the Facebook parent reported its first cash outflow in more than a decade amid concerns over its AI-related expenditures. In premarket trading on Friday, CoreWeave rose 2 per cent, while 'Magnificent 7' stocks were mixed, with up 0.7 per cent and Microsoft down 0.6 per cent. At 06:09 a.m. ET, Dow E-minis were down 308 points, or 0.58 per cent, and S&P 500 E-minis were down 15.5 points, or 0.2 per cent. Nasdaq 100 E-minis were down 0.75 points, or flat. Brent crude held near a more than five-month high amid Middle East supply concerns, adding to inflation worries ahead of the Federal Reserve's policy meeting next week. Nasdaq was on track for a weekly loss, while the benchmark S&P 500 and the blue-chip Dow remained higher for the week, supported by gains in defensive sectors as investors sought refuge from the volatility in technology stocks. Market focus remains on the earnings season. American Express and SLB, among others, are set to report later in the day. S&P 500's third-quarter profit growth is now forecast at 32.3 per cent, up from 30.7 per cent previously, according to LSEG data. In other premarket moves, gold miner Newmont fell 1.5 per cent after reporting quarterly results and warning that unit costs are expected to trend higher in 2027. Bloom Energy rose 1.7 per cent after the energy firm raised its fiscal 2026 forecast.

In a cave in South Sulawesi's Maros-Pangkep, an artwork depicting human-like figures interacting with a pig was dated by researchers from Australia's Griffith University to be at least 51,200 years old.

MAROS-PANGKEP, Indonesia: The world's oldest cave paintings on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi are under threat as heat and smoke from the country's worst wildfires in more than a decade risk accelerating the deterioration of the more than 67,000-year-old works of art, researchers said. Indonesia is battling its most intense forest and land fires since 2015 as a severe El Nino drives up temperatures and reduces rainfall, leaving its forest and peatland vulnerable to fire. While the islands of Sumatra and Borneo are the worst affected by the disaster, fires have also spread on the island of Sulawesi, including in South Sulawesi where limestone caves house the world's oldest prehistoric art.  In a cave in South Sulawesi's Maros-Pangkep, an artwork depicting human-like figures interacting with a pig was dated by researchers from Australia's Griffith University to be at least 51,200 years old. In a cave on Muna island, off Sulawesi, a reddish-coloured hand stencil was dated to at least 67,800 years.

Near the Maros-Pangkep cave, firefighters worked to put out fires as smoke drifted over the dramatic karst landscape that is a defining feature of the national park and UNESCO Global Geopark surrounding the cave. Firefighter Muhammad Ikfar said fires burned near the site for more than a week earlier this month and came within 800m of the cave. More than 270 hectares of the national park burned between Sep 30 and Oct 18, Ikfar said.  "The first and most destructive effect is the heat. Even without direct fire touching the paintings, it could ruin them because it changes the temperature around the paintings and accelerates the process of corrosion," said Griffith University archaeologist Basran Burhan. The smoke also creates soot. "They create soot on the paintings and cover them, so that the paintings will become blurred and difficult to identify," he said. On Thursday (Oct 22) and Friday, firefighters were working to put out fires in other parts of the park, firefighter Ikfar said, adding that the conditions were dry with no rain yet. "If we don't do something about this quick, if there isn't any tactical mitigation efforts for this incident we will lose one of the most amazing evidence of human history in Maros-Pangkep," Burhan said. "And that is a great shame."

NEW YORK, Oct 23 : US stock investors face a pivotal week, with corporate earnings reports led by major AI players and a Federal Reserve meeting both posing critical tests for a suddenly shaky market rally. Weakness in technology shares left investors on edge about the state of the AI trade that has driven the US equity bull market that just marked its fourth anniversary. The AI pullback deepened on Thursday, with the Nasdaq Composite posting its biggest one-day drop since June. Investors were disappointed by quarterly reports from Meta and Lam Research. Meta is one of the hyperscalers spending massively to build out data centers, while Lam is a high-flying semiconductor company, one of a group that has been among the biggest AI stock winners. Three other hyperscalers - Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon - headline a packed week of quarterly results, including about one-third of S&P 500 companies. The Fed's interest rate policy meeting on Wednesday also could rattle markets.

"There are a lot of balls in the air," said Nick Giorgi, chief equity strategist at Alpine Macro.  "Next week, you have a lot more tech earnings, and right now the market is taking a discerning eye as it relates to all the spending that goes along with artificial intelligence," Giorgi said. "The market's just not giving the benefit of the doubt to companies that are spending a ton of money on building this all out, which to us is actually very healthy, but still does augur for some short-term pain." Investors also have their focus trained on the US midterm elections on November 3, with growing bets that the Democrats will wrest control of the US Congress away from President Donald Trump's Republican party. The series of market catalysts could ratchet up volatility over the next couple of weeks and challenge optimism that has helped lift the benchmark S&P 500 index up about 12 per cent in 2026. HYPERSCALERS ON THE HOT SEAT Robust US profit growth has underpinned the stock market's gains this year in the face of headwinds including spiking Treasury yields and rising energy costs stemming from the Middle East conflict. With more than 100 companies having posted results so far, third-quarter S&P 500 earnings are on pace to have climbed more than 32 per cent from a year ago, according to LSEG IBES data. Next week is the busiest of the reporting season. "I think earnings will determine whether this ... tech pullback is a buying opportunity, or is there a deeper correction ahead," said King Lip, chief strategist at BakerAvenue Wealth Management. "What we need is just another round of really strong earnings." Alphabet and Microsoft report on Wednesday. Amazon's results are due Thursday. Focus will be on the guidance the companies give on capital spending plans and whether they are seeing returns on the massive outlays. Capital spending from hyperscalers, expected to be around $800 billion this year, is boosting the bottom lines for a wide swath of companies involved in the AI buildout. But investors are wary of the sustainability of such spending amid mounting financing costs. "Earnings are critical to the overall confidence level of the AI trade and how much longer the spend will continue," said Kevin Mahn, president and chief investment officer at Hennion & Walsh Asset Management. FED EXPECTED TO PAUSE ON RATES, FOR NOW Quarterly reports next week from chip companies Intel and Sandisk also could influence the AI trade. Elsewhere, other high-profile companies set to report next week include drugmaker Eli Lilly, oil majors Exxon and Chevron and industrial equipment giant Caterpillar.  The prospect for more interest rate hikes also comes into focus with the Fed meeting. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, in an effort to control above-target inflation, but Fed fund futures late on Thursday suggested only a 5 per cent chance the Fed will hike again when it gives its policy statement on Wednesday, according to LSEG data.  One factor: Investors are dubious that the Fed will want to increase rates just a week before the midterm elections. However, markets are leaning toward a hike at the next meeting in December, with futures suggesting an 80 per cent probability of such a move then. Walter Todd, chief investment officer at Greenwood Capital, said he will be watching for any hints about the rate path at Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference following the decision.  "Does he say something to give an idea about December, because right now the expectation is there is going to be a hike?" Todd said.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Oct 23 : Private plaintiffs' lawyers stand to collect up to $1.27 billion from New Mexico if the state's $25 billion court win against Meta Platforms this week is upheld, according to a Reuters review of a contract with the state.  New Mexico hired Chicago-based law firm DiCello Levitt to represent it in the Meta case, which alleged the tech company duped its users about who had access to their personal data on its Facebook platform. The state's 2025 contract with DiCello Levitt, reviewed by Reuters after a records request, says the firm can ask the judge overseeing the case to award it 20 per cent of the first $50 million of any eventual recovery, 15 per cent of the next $50 million, 10 per cent of the next $150 million and 5 per cent of any amounts over $250 million.  New Mexico and other states have turned to private law firms in a growing number of cases against major technology companies to buttress their legal teams against deep-pocketed defendants. The outside lawyers typically don't charge by the hour but are entitled to a cut of any winnings.

In the Meta case, a jury sided with the state in September, and a judge on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25 billion. Meta denied wrongdoing and said it will appeal. Legal experts including Villanova University law professor Peter Ormerod told Reuters this week that the company has a strong basis for arguing that the judgment should be reduced.  If New Mexico ultimately recovers $25 billion from Meta, DiCello Levitt's fees could reach $1.27 billion under the law firm's contract. The amount would come out of the funds Meta pays to New Mexico.    UNCERTAINTY OVER FINAL PAYOUT To be sure, Meta could win its appeal or the judgment could be trimmed, and the court is not obligated to award the firm the maximum fees allowed under its contract. DiCello Levitt declined to comment about its fees. New Mexico's lead lawyer at the firm, Corban Rhodes, in a statement called the court's decision a "defining moment for consumer protection and privacy." Randi McGinn, a New Mexico lawyer who worked with the DiCello firm in representing the state, told Reuters her small Albuquerque firm is entitled to collect about 33 per cent of its fees. DiCello's contract allowed the firm to designate other lawyers as subcontractors. McGinn, who delivered the state's opening statement and closing argument, cautioned that a final outcome in the case could take several years. “People will say it’s a lot of money. But the truth is, we won’t see any of that money unless we win an appeal,” McGinn said.  Contingency fee awards over $1 billion are exceedingly rare, said Fordham University law professor Howard Erichson. While New Mexico's contract caps fees for DiCello Levitt near 5 per cent, "the sheer size of the recovery means it could result in a massive fee here, so I would expect the court to examine it carefully," Erichson said. The New Mexico attorney general's office and a Meta spokesperson did not immediately respond to requests for comment about the legal fees. STATES TURN TO PRIVATE FIRMS Some companies and business groups say that giving private lawyers a stake in state enforcement actions can put lawyers' financial interests in conflict with public policy concerns. Defenders of the practice counter that it helps level the playing field for states going up against companies that can afford armies of lawyers.  The rewards can be substantial. Norton Rose Fulbright is set to receive more than $156 million in legal fees for representing Texas in a consumer privacy case that Google settled for $1.375 billion. Law firms Keller Postman and McKool Smith billed Texas $142.6 million in a consumer privacy lawsuit against Meta that led to a $1.4 billion settlement in 2024. DiCello Levitt's contract mirrors one between New Mexico and Motley Rice for a separate lawsuit alleging Meta fostered social media addiction and other harms on its platforms. Meta denies the claims. Motley Rice could seek up to $67.1 million in that case if appeals courts uphold a pair of rulings totaling $942 million against Meta. Wednesday’s ruling came in a case New Mexico filed in 2021 against Meta after disclosures that British political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica obtained data from as many as 87 million Facebook users without their consent. The now-defunct Cambridge Analytica used the data for voter profiling and targeting.

Source: Reuters

Oct 23 : MotoGP will forge ahead with next month's Qatar Grand Prix despite Middle East tensions and concerns from some riders over safety, while others said they trusted organisers Dorna to ensure the race could be staged safely. The race at the Lusail International Circuit, originally scheduled for April but postponed to November 6-8 due to the regional conflict, remains on the calendar for what would be the 20th round of the season. Several sports events in Saudi Arabia, including the Saudi International golf tournament, the Urban Cycling World Championships and the FIFAe World Cup, were scrapped earlier this month after a strike on Riyadh's international airport killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300. Earlier this week, the US State Department ordered some diplomats and family members to depart from its missions in Saudi Arabia and plans to withdraw family members from a number of other US missions in the region.

However, a MotoGP source told Reuters the Qatar Grand Prix remains on the calendar and preparations continue, adding that the safety and wellbeing of everyone involved was their first priority. ALEX MARQUEZ VOICES SCEPTICISM Gresini Racing's Alex Marquez, who finished runner-up in the championship last season, voiced scepticism about whether safety could truly be guaranteed in such a volatile environment. "Every day, it (the situation) changes and every day it looks worse. That's how it is," the Spaniard said ahead of this weekend's Australian Grand Prix. "The championship tells us that everything is under control, but I think nobody has a situation like that under control. It's quite complex. "From one day to the next, everything can change a lot, and I think it's not a decision they should make now. They should be realistic and wait for the next few days." Formula One is also planning to host the season's last two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi as planned, with International Automobile Federation (FIA) president Mohammed Ben Sulayem saying the situation was currently "fine" in the region. Liberty Media, which acquired the F1 commercial rights in 2017, took over MotoGP's parent company Dorna in 2024. "For sure it is a lot of money on the deal and Dorna wants everything. It's like that," Marquez added. "But also with the health of everybody they need to take care as well, because many people will go there." CHAMPIONSHIP LEADER MARTIN KEEN TO RACE While the Formula One championship could be wrapped up before the final two races of the season - with Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli holding a 102-point lead - the MotoGP title race remains razor-tight after 17 of the 22 rounds. Aprilia's Jorge Martin holds a two-point lead over Ducati's reigning champion Marc Marquez ahead of this weekend's action at the Phillip Island Circuit. "I want to go to Qatar because the circuit is incredible. I believe in the championship and in what those who manage it decide," Martin said. "Nobody has said we're not going. It's just another race. If we go, great. If not, that's fine too. If the organisers decide we can go, it'll be because our safety is guaranteed." The Qatar Grand Prix has been a near-constant fixture on the MotoGP calendar since its debut in 2004, with the only interruption coming in 2020 when the race was cancelled due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

WASHINGTON, Oct 23 : People can readily share images and sounds digitally, as evidenced by the billions of smartphones in use globally that often overload the human senses of sight and hearing. But smell generally remains missing from remote communication. That could soon change. Researchers have developed technology that features an electronic nose that recognizes certain smells, like the distinctive aroma of coffee, and then instructs a small and wearable remote device to release scent molecules matching it. The digital communication can take place at any distance, from across the room to around the world. "In simple terms, it connects 'smelling something here' with 'recreating the corresponding smell somewhere else,'" said Chunyu Yang, an Ohio State University doctoral student in materials science and engineering and lead author of a study describing the technology published in the journal Science Advances. "The idea is to add smell to the visual and audio information we already share remotely, making those experiences more engaging," Yang said.

The researchers call this latest development in the field of digital scent technology "Scentronic." "What makes Scentronic different is that it brings odor sensing and generation together for remote sharing. To the best of our knowledge, our study is the first to explore this integration in a compact platform for remote odor sharing," Yang said. The researchers created an e-nose, a device that uses an array of gas sensors to detect chemical compounds associated with different odors. A machine-learning model then classifies odors that the e-nose has been trained to recognize — beer, cake, coffee, oranges and red wine. The technology uses an online platform to transmit the odor information to a scent generator, which then releases fragrances to recreate the aroma at the receiving end. The scent molecules themselves are not transmitted over the internet. The e-nose device is roughly 6 inches (15 cm) in diameter and is portable, though not designed to be worn. The researchers developed several versions of the odor generator, including wristband, necklace and handheld designs. 'EVERYDAY ODORS' At this point, the e-nose recognizes just the five scents. "We chose these because they are familiar everyday odors with different scent profiles, making them useful examples for demonstrating the system. We have not yet expanded beyond those categories," Yang said. "A broader scent library is possible in principle, but an unlimited repertoire is far beyond what we have demonstrated. Recognizing an odor and accurately reproducing it are separate challenges. Covering a useful range of everyday scents is a more realistic goal, although that would still require substantial development," Yang said. The receiving device cannot recreate every smell Scentronic encounters.  "To support additional odors, we would need to train the electronic nose to recognize them and provide corresponding scented liquids in the odor generator," Yang said. The researchers see various potential applications for the technology. "For example, someone could share the scent of a meal with family or friends who live far away. Other potential applications include more immersive virtual and augmented reality experiences and online shopping that allows customers to sample selected scents remotely," Yang said. 'A RESEARCH PROTOTYPE' The research was conducted and the devices developed without the involvement of a company, Yang said. "At present, this is a research prototype. Moving toward commercialization would require a larger, more diverse training dataset and reliable odor recognition under real-world conditions, where smells often occur in mixtures," Yang said. "The odor generator would also need further development to support more scents while remaining compact and convenient to use. Other considerations include scent fidelity, refillability, durability, manufacturing costs and the safety of repeated exposure to the scented mist," Yang said. Smartphones are becoming increasingly capable. Could they in the future incorporate scent technology so that, for instance, a person at a tailgate party before an Ohio State football game could call a friend and share video, audio and the aroma of hot dogs on the grill? "In principle, a smartphone could connect to a scent-generating accessory. Integrating everything into the phone itself would be more challenging because the scent reservoirs, electronics and atomizers all take up space and add weight. Miniaturization and convenient refilling would be important considerations," Yang said. "The tailgate example illustrates the idea well. A future system could potentially combine video and audio with a corresponding scent, provided it could recognize the relevant odor and the receiver had a suitable scent formulation available. Our current system has not demonstrated the transmission of a grilling-hot-dog scent or the exact mixture of smells at a tailgate party," Yang said.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Oct 23 : Advances in artificial intelligence have uncovered a stream of new software vulnerabilities that are almost certain to trigger more disruption along the lines of the outages that percolated across global government websites this week, according to seven cybersecurity professionals who spoke to Reuters. AI helped drive a doubling of the number of digital flaws discovered year-on-year, according to research due to be published in the coming days by VulnCheck, a Massachusetts-based threat intelligence firm. Matthew Prince, the chief executive of the digital infrastructure firm Cloudflare, told Reuters he was aware of “a bunch of additional severe vulnerabilities that are present in other pieces of critical software” and predicted busy months ahead as AI surfaced long-hidden weaknesses in the fabric of the internet.   “I think we’re going to have a couple years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling,” Prince said in an interview on Thursday.

The outages that spread across government sites in Europe and elsewhere beginning on Wednesday happened after the discovery of weaknesses in PHP, a venerable programming language that powers a huge swath of the internet. Operators have been rushing to fix their software in anticipation of mass exploitation and, because some felt they could not patch before hackers jumped in, a subset simply yanked their sites offline until they could make them safe. VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity said the scramble to fix PHP came during an already busy week in cybersecurity. The week also brought disclosures of vulnerabilities PHP alternative Node.js and streaming program Plex, breaches tied to AI gateway LiteLLM and development platform Railway, and the revelation that the Indian certificate authority eMudhra had used an extraordinarily flimsy cryptographic key that potentially put users across the internet at risk. “If we just saw four or five things like this, this week, I would expect we’re going to see a lot more,” Garrity said. “I think there’s going to be a lot more fire drills for anything that’s internet exposed.” TIMELINES SHORTENING  The codebases that run modern programs are sprawling and mistakes, or “bugs,” that open up potential avenues for exploitation often crop up in unexpected places.  Previously, finding bugs required a baseline level of skill, and taking advantage of those bugs to build digital lockpicks – called “exploits” – could be expected to take weeks or months of work by an experienced professional. That would in the past have provided defenders a little breathing room to fix bugs and gently roll out software updates. AI has effectively thrown those assumptions out the window. Models can find one bug after another by subjecting codebases to round-the-clock scrutiny, and can turn around exploits in hours. Shane Fry, the chief technology officer of Virginia-based RunSafe Security, said the demonstrated performance of AI models over the past few months had effectively laid to rest any doubts over whether they would change the industry. “What's fundamentally, and unquestionably, changing is the timescale for not only finding vulnerabilities, but how quickly adversaries can weaponize them,” Fry said.  SCARY MONSTERS While all the experts Reuters spoke to agreed that defenders’ timelines were getting shorter, they were split on whether AI would lead to a hacker free-for-all. Daniel Stenberg, the lead developer of the file transfer tool curl, argued the vulnerabilities found by AI models tended to be exotic bugs that were difficult for rogue actors to take advantage of. Ramy Rahman, a senior principal solutions engineer at cybersecurity company ArmorCode, said “more disclosed vulnerabilities do not automatically mean more successful attacks." There was tentative evidence of that around the PHP vulnerability that drew worldwide concern this week. Threat intelligence firm Hunt.io said that – like Amazon and Cloudflare – it had seen aggressive attempts to take advantage of the bug. But the firm’s head of research, Esteban Borges, said that, as of 2 p.m. Eastern Time on Thursday (1800 GMT), the cybercriminals he tracked appeared to have failed to cobble together a working tool to take advantage of it. Prince, of Cloudflare, told Reuters he had seen anecdotal evidence of compromises linked to the PHP vulnerability.  The deluge of AI-driven discoveries might rattle the industry, but would be a net positive in the end, he said, comparing it to slaying the monsters in a haunted house. The confrontation might be scary, he said, but leaving the monsters to lurk quietly behind closed doors was far worse.  “The reality is, we’re going to get a lot of this stuff cleaned up,” he said.

Source: Reuters
